**Challenging the Assumption: CISA's Open-Source Guidance**

Everyone says that CISA's new guidance on using open-source software is a no-brainer: "You must assess and mitigate risks associated with open-source dependencies." I disagree. While risk assessment is crucial, the guidance oversimplifies the complexities of open-source software development.

Here are a few reasons why I think this common belief is incomplete:

• **Open-source software is not inherently more vulnerable**: While open-source code can be more susceptible to vulnerabilities, many commercial software solutions have their own set of risks. A one-size-fits-all approach is not effective.

• **Risk assessment is more nuanced than just counting dependencies**: The quality of dependencies, the maturity of the open-source project, and the level of community engagement all play a critical role in determining risk. A simple count of dependencies is not a reliable metric.

• **The guidance overlooks the benefits of open-source**: Open-source software can provide greater transparency, community-driven development, and cost savings. These benefits should not be dismissed in favor of blanket risk mitigation.

• **Commercial software often has its own set of dependencies**: Commercial software often relies on open-source components, which can introduce similar risks. A more nuanced approach is needed.

• **Open-source software can be a strategic advantage**: In some cases, using open-source software can provide a competitive advantage by allowing organizations to customize and adapt the code to their specific needs.

When might the common belief still apply? When organizations are using high-risk open-source dependencies without adequate oversight, or when they are not adequately tracking and managing their dependencies.

What are your thoughts on the trade-offs between risk assessment and the benefits of open-source software?
